title: Daily Health Briefing
intro: Good morning! Today's digest pulls fresh angles across your five tracked topics — the largest human rapamycin trial getting underway, HIIT in recreationally active women, home-based pelvic-floor biofeedback, immunotherapy + vaccine strategies for HER2+ breast cancer, and where sleep guidelines now land on drugs vs. behavior. Sources (PubMed, JAMA, NIH/PMC, AASM, ASCO) are linked as chips under each section.

sections.body:
The headline in longevity medicine right now is **scale**: after the 48-week PEARL trial, the field is moving to a far larger, longer test of **low-dose rapamycin (an mTOR inhibitor)**.

- A new **University of Arizona RCT** is enrolling **720 adults aged 65+** for **weekly low-dose rapamycin (~8 mg) vs. placebo over 2 years**, with a 3rd year of follow-up. Crucially, it uses *real clinical endpoints* — **frailty and systemic inflammation** — plus deep genetic/epigenetic/immune phenotyping. This is a step up from PEARL (48 weeks) and the earlier Mannick immune studies (6 weeks).
- Sober framing on the evidence: a 2026 evidence-grading review puts **rapamycin/mTOR inhibition at the top tier (B)** of any longevity molecule — driven by two completed RCTs showing better vaccine response and fewer infections in older adults — but stresses **there is still no human lifespan trial**.
- **NAD+ precursors (NMN/NR)** grade lower (C): they reliably *raise blood NAD+* and one RCT improved insulin sensitivity in prediabetic women, but **clinical healthspan/lifespan outcomes don't yet exist**. **Senolytics** (dasatinib+quercetin, fisetin) remain early with small human data.

Practical takeaways: benefits so far are **modest and often sex-specific**; treat single-supplement "longevity" marketing skeptically; and note that any rapamycin use for aging is **off-label and warrants physician oversight + lab monitoring**.

sections.body:
Two recent meta-analyses converge on the same message for women: **HIIT is a time-efficient way to raise cardiorespiratory fitness — but it is not a stand-alone fix for strength or fat loss.**

- A **2025 systematic review & meta-analysis** (Scientific Reports) in **recreationally active females** found HIIT produced a *large* improvement in **VO2peak** (g = 1.27, 95% CI 0.62–1.93) and a smaller-but-significant gain in **VO2max** (g = 0.40). It also **modestly lowered body-fat percentage** (g ≈ −0.30) — but showed **no significant change in total body mass or fat mass**, i.e. body-composition benefits are real but limited.
- A **2026 review of 19 RCTs** in middle-aged and older women found HIIT **significantly improves VO2max** (SMD = 1.20, 95% CI 0.86–1.54, *high certainty*), consistent across age and body-mass status — **but no significant gain in muscle strength** on its own.

Bottom line: intensity drives the aerobic gains at a low time cost. To also build strength/lean mass and reshape body composition, **pair HIIT with resistance training** and manage intensity, progression, and recovery — especially important in peri-/post-menopause.

sections.body:
**Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT)** remains the evidence-based **first-line** treatment for stress urinary incontinence (SUI) — and the newest angle is about *doing it correctly*, with **biofeedback** to confirm activation.

- A **JAMA Network Open multicenter RCT** tested a **home-based, pressure-mediated biofeedback device + PFMT** in postpartum women with new-onset SUI. Adding the biofeedback device helped women perform contractions correctly and improved outcomes vs. PFMT instruction alone — reinforcing that *technique and adherence matter more than raw reps*.
- Complementary 2026 evidence: the **PEFLOW** prenatal program (764 first-time mothers, 9 hospitals) **cut 6-week postpartum SUI from 13.9% to 8.7%** and more than doubled the share of women achieving strong pelvic-floor strength (Modified Oxford Scale ≥4: 17.8% vs. 7.9%).

Key point: a supervised or **biofeedback-guided** program tends to beat unsupervised effort. If you're unsure you're isolating the right muscles, confirm activation with a pelvic-health clinician or a validated device before scaling up volume.

sections.body:
Two fronts are advancing for **HER2-positive breast cancer**, including the hard-to-treat **TP53/p53 co-mutated** subset.

**1. Immunotherapy & vaccines (ASCO 2026).**
- **DESTINY-Breast07** tested **trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd / Enhertu) + durvalumab** (a PD-L1 immunotherapy) as *first-line* therapy for HER2+ metastatic disease, reporting an **82.8% objective response rate** and **median progression-free survival of 37.7 months** — encouraging, though biomarkers to select responders are still needed.
- The **HER2 multi-epitope peptide vaccine (H2NVAC)** given *with* T-DM1 in residual HER2+ disease was **well-tolerated with no dose-limiting toxicities** in a safety run-in, and is now in a randomized placebo-controlled **phase 2 trial (NCT04197687)**.
- In early-stage disease, the phase 2 **neoHIP** trial reported **100% event-free survival at ~37 months** with neoadjuvant THP + pembrolizumab.

**2. Exploiting the p53 vulnerability.**
- A mechanistic study (PubMed/PMC, 2025) showed **HER2;p53 co-mutant** tumors are **resistant to neratinib alone** but — because they carry more open chromatin and hyper-transcribe DNA-repair genes — are **sensitive to the TOP1-inhibitor payload in T-DXd**. **Neratinib + T-DXd** was highly effective preclinically and is being tested in a phase 1 trial (**NCI ETCTN 10495 / NCT05372614**).

Important framing: these are **investigational** options. "Alternative" here should mean *evidence-based, trial-based options discussed with an oncologist* — not a replacement for standard care. p53 itself remains largely **undruggable**, with no approved p53-targeted therapy yet.

sections.body:
For restless or fragmented sleep, 2026 guidance keeps **behavioral therapy ahead of pills and supplements**.

- The **AASM's 2026 combination-treatment guideline** concluded that **CBT-I + medication beats medication alone**, but is **not better than CBT-I alone** — so **CBT-I remains first-line** for chronic insomnia, delivered individually, in groups, or **digitally**.
- A **2026 clinical review** frames pharmacotherapy as second-line and time-limited: **Z-drugs** lose efficacy and carry parasomnia/cognitive/misuse risks (keep to ≤4 weeks); **prolonged-release melatonin (2 mg)** shows only **modest** benefit, mainly in adults **>55** or mild sleep-onset insomnia; and newer **dual orexin receptor antagonists (DORAs)** offer better tolerability and less cognitive hangover, though long-term data are still limited.
- On supplements: fast-release melatonin is **not recommended** except when a **circadian** issue (jet lag, shift work) is involved; **magnesium** evidence is limited/preliminary.

Best-practice habits for disjointed sleep:

1. Hold a **fixed wake time**, 7 days a week.
2. Use the bed **only for sleep**; if awake ~20 min, get up and reset (stimulus control).
3. Consider **sleep restriction** to consolidate fragmented sleep (ideally clinician-guided).
4. Dim lights and cut screens in a wind-down window; keep the room cool, dark, quiet.
5. If it persists beyond a few weeks, see a provider to rule out **sleep apnea** and start **CBT-I**.
